name: Sardines, Lemon, Oil
why: The most important food in the program, eaten the way it costs the least effort. If you do nothing else, do this.
steps: Open the tin. Tip the fish onto a plate with the oil it came in.
Squeeze the lemon over. Add another pour of olive oil on top of the tin's own.
Salt, more than feels right.
Sauerkraut on the side, cold, straight from the jar.

name: Sardines on Charred Greens
why: The char takes the raw edge off the greens and gives the whole plate a savoury base that you would otherwise need a sauce for.
steps: Get a dry pan as hot as it goes. No oil yet.
Throw the greens in dry. Leave them. Do not stir. Wait until the edges go black in patches, about 90 seconds.
Now add butter and the sliced garlic, and toss for 30 seconds off the heat.
Tip onto a plate, lay the sardines over the top with their oil, lemon, salt.

name: The Slow Fold
why: A French omelette is the test of whether you can control a pan. Low heat and constant movement, and it will be custard instead of rubber.
steps: Beat the eggs hard with salt until completely uniform, no streaks of white.
Melt butter in a non-stick pan over the lowest heat that will still melt it. Do not let it brown.
Pour in the eggs and stir constantly with a spatula, scraping the base, for about two minutes. It should look like loose curds.
Stop stirring. Let it set for 20 seconds, then tilt the pan and roll it over on itself.
Slide onto a plate seam-side down. Herbs, and a little more butter on top.

name: Eggs Confit in Olive Oil
why: Cooked in fat at low heat the whites go silky rather than squeaky, and the oil afterwards is flavored for everything else that week.
ing: Enough olive oil to cover, about 250ml
steps: Put the oil, garlic and herbs in a small pan. Bring it to just barely warm, around 130°C, which is well below a sizzle.
Crack the eggs in gently, one at a time.
Hold it there for 6 to 8 minutes. The white sets, the yolk stays liquid, nothing browns.
Lift out with a slotted spoon. Salt heavily.
Strain the oil into a jar once cool. That is now your cooking oil for the week.

name: Charred Leek and Egg
why: The dark green tops of a leek normally go in the bin. Charred hard, they are the best-tasting part of the vegetable.
steps: Cut the dark tops off the leek and keep them. Split the white part lengthwise and rinse.
Char the dark tops in a dry, very hot pan until they are properly black. Chop them fine and set aside as a seasoning.
Cook the white part cut-side down in butter, low, for 10 minutes until it gives to a knife.
Fry the eggs in the same pan.
Plate the leek, eggs over, then the blackened tops scattered on top with salt, oil and a splash of vinegar.

name: Liver and Onions, Morning
why: Your weekly liver, handled so it is not gray. Dense in almost everything the panel measures, and cheapest of all the animal foods.
steps: Salt the liver and leave it on the counter for 10 minutes while you cook the onions.
Cook the onions slowly in butter until brown and sweet, about 10 minutes.
Push them aside, raise the heat, and sear the liver for 60 to 90 seconds a side. No longer. It should still be pink inside.
Take it off, splash vinegar into the hot pan, and pour that over.
Rest for two minutes before eating.

name: Cold Salmon, Mustard, Herbs
why: A restaurant kitchen never cooks one portion. Cook extra salmon at dinner and the first meal the next day takes no time at all.
steps: Take the salmon out of the fridge while the kettle boils. Cold fish tastes of nothing.
Flake it into large pieces onto the plate. Do not shred it.
Mix mustard, olive oil and lemon into a loose dressing with a fork.
Spoon over, add sliced cucumber, herbs and salt.

name: Broth with a Dropped Egg
why: On a morning with no appetite, this goes down when nothing else will, and it still carries protein, minerals and collagen.
steps: Bring the broth to a bare simmer with the ginger. Never a rolling boil.
Stir it into a slow whirlpool and drop the egg into the middle. Leave it for three minutes.
Add the spinach for the last 30 seconds.
Coconut aminos and salt to finish. Drink it from a mug if you would rather.

name: Mackerel, Mustard, Radish
why: Mackerel carries more omega-3 per gram than almost anything else you can buy, and it is one of the cheapest fish at the counter.
steps: Salt the skin and leave it 5 minutes, then pat it completely dry. Wet skin will not crisp.
Ghee in a hot pan. Fish skin-side down, and press it flat for the first 10 seconds.
Leave it for 3 minutes without moving it. Turn, 30 seconds, out.
Toss the radishes with vinegar and salt while the fish rests.
Mustard on the plate, fish on top, radishes alongside.

name: Broccoli Stem Hash
why: The stem is the sweetest part of the broccoli and the part most people throw out. Peeled and diced it behaves like a potato.
steps: Peel the tough outer skin off the stems with a knife. Dice what is left into small cubes.
Get the tallow hot. Add the stems and onion in one layer and leave them to color before stirring, about 4 minutes.
Stir, add garlic, cook another 5 minutes until tender at the edges and browned.
Make two wells, crack the eggs in, cover, 3 minutes.
Salt and pepper, straight from the pan.

name: Eggs Baked in Mushrooms
why: Large flat mushrooms hold an egg and their own liquid, so nothing needs a dish and nothing needs washing.
steps: Take the stems out and sit the mushrooms gill-side up in a pan. Butter, garlic and thyme in each cup.
Low heat, lid on, for 8 minutes. They will release a lot of liquid. Leave it.
Crack an egg into each one.
Lid back on, another 6 to 8 minutes until the white is set.
Salt. A little grated hard cheese if your tier allows it.

name: Avocado, Sardine, Salt
why: Potassium, fat and DHA in one plate with nothing to wash up. The fastest compliant meal in the book.
steps: Halve the avocado and score the flesh in the skin.
Break the sardines over it, oil and all.
Lemon, olive oil, a heavy pinch of salt, pepper.
Eat it out of the skin with a spoon.

name: Kimchi and Eggs
why: A live ferment beside eggs, which is two of the daily list in one pan and the easiest way to get a forkful in before noon.
steps: Fry the kimchi in butter for 2 minutes until the edges catch. This is where the flavor comes from.
Push it to the side of the pan.
Beat the eggs with salt and pour them into the empty half. Stir slowly over low heat.
Fold the kimchi through at the last moment, not before.
Coconut aminos, spring onion, off the heat.

name: Charred Cabbage, Anchovy Butter
why: Anchovy melts into butter and disappears, leaving savouriness with no sugar and nothing from a bottle. Keep a log of it in the freezer.
steps: Mash the anchovies and a grated clove of garlic into soft butter with a fork. That is the anchovy butter.
Cut the cabbage into two thick wedges through the core so they hold together.
Dry pan, high heat, cut face down. Leave it for 4 minutes until black.
Turn, drop in a spoon of the butter, cover, and cook 6 minutes more until a knife goes through.
Another spoon of the butter over the top, lemon, salt. Fry an egg in the same pan if you want it.

name: Steak and Eggs, Second Day
why: Leftover steak reheated hot goes gray and tough. Warmed gently in butter it is better than it was the night before.
steps: Slice the steak cold, against the grain, while it is still firm.
Melt butter in a pan on the lowest heat. Lay the slices in and turn them once. Thirty seconds a side is plenty, you are warming not cooking.
Lift them out onto the plate immediately.
Fry the eggs in the same butter.
Greens alongside with olive oil and salt.

name: Brined Zucchini and Egg
why: Zucchini is mostly water, which is why it usually goes soggy. Salt it in advance and it griddles instead of steaming.
steps: Slice the zucchini into thick planks. Salt both sides generously and lay them in a colander for two hours. Do this the night before.
Pat them completely dry. A lot of water will have come out.
Dry griddle or heavy pan, very hot, no oil. Three minutes a side until there are black bars on them.
Fry the eggs separately in olive oil.
Plate together, lemon, olive oil, herbs, pepper.

name: Oysters to Start the Day
why: Nothing else on the list carries zinc and selenium like an oyster, and they need no cooking at all. Buy them closed and heavy.
steps: Mix the shallot with a spoon of vinegar and leave it while you shuck.
Hold each oyster in a folded towel, hinge towards you, and work the knife into the hinge with a twist, not a stab.
Run the knife along the top shell to cut the muscle, then under the oyster to free it.
Check for shell fragments. Keep all the liquor.
Lemon or the shallot vinegar, pepper, and do not drown them.

name: Asparagus, Egg, Brown Butter
why: Butter cooked past melting turns nutty and completely changes what it does to a plate. It takes ninety seconds and most people never do it.
steps: Snap the woody ends off the asparagus. They break where they want to.
Char them in a dry hot pan, rolling, for 4 minutes until blistered.
In a separate small pan melt the butter and keep going past the foam until the solids at the bottom turn brown and it smells like nuts. Take it off immediately.
Soft-boil or fry the eggs.
Asparagus on the plate, egg on top, brown butter poured over, lemon and salt.

name: Sweet Potato and Egg Hash
why: For the tiers that still have starch. Par-cooking first means the outside crisps before the inside is raw, which is the whole trick.
steps: Dice the sweet potato and boil it for 4 minutes only. Drain it and let it steam dry in the colander.
Get the tallow properly hot. Add the potato in one layer and leave it alone for 5 minutes.
Turn once, add the onion, cook another 5 minutes. Garlic in the last minute.
Wells for the eggs, cover, 3 minutes.
Salt and pepper. This is a midday meal, not an everyday one.

name: Berries Beside Eggs
why: Berries only, in season, and never on their own. Fruit with fat and protein beside it lands very differently to fruit by itself.
ing: Handful of blueberries or raspberries, in season
steps: Cook the eggs first, soft, in butter, with salt.
Put the berries on the same plate, not in a separate bowl. They are part of the meal.
Crush a few nuts over them.
A little cinnamon. Nothing else, and nothing sweet added.
Out of season, leave the berries off and eat the eggs.

name: Salmon Collar, Garlic Butter
why: The collar is the piece behind the gills, thrown away at industrial scale and richer in fat than the fillet. Ask your fish counter for them and they are close to free.
steps: Salt the collars on both sides and leave them 20 minutes while the oven heats to 220°C.
Roast skin-side up, 12 to 14 minutes, until the skin blisters and the fat runs.
Melt the butter with crushed garlic in a small pan, low, until the garlic softens but does not color.
Pour the garlic butter over the collars straight out of the oven.
Lemon, parsley, pepper. Eat them with your hands and get into the corners.

name: Whole Roast Mackerel
why: A whole fish cooks more evenly than a fillet because the bones conduct heat and the skin holds the moisture in. It also costs less.
steps: Score the skin three times on each side, down to the bone but not through it. This is what stops it curling.
Salt inside and out, heavily, 20 minutes ahead.
Stuff the cavity with lemon slices, garlic and herbs.
Lay it on the sliced fennel or celery in a hot oven at 220°C for 18 to 20 minutes.
The eye goes white and the flesh comes away from the bone when it is done. Olive oil over it at the table.

name: Reverse-Sear Ribeye
why: Low oven first, hard pan second. The whole steak comes out one color instead of gray-banded, and you cannot overshoot it.
steps: Salt the steak all over and leave it uncovered in the fridge overnight if you can, an hour if you cannot.
Oven at 110°C. Steak on a rack, 25 to 35 minutes, until the middle reads 48°C.
Rest it 10 minutes out of the oven while a heavy pan gets as hot as it will go with tallow in it.
Sear 60 seconds a side. Add butter, garlic and thyme, tilt the pan and spoon it over for 30 seconds more.
Rest again for 5 minutes. Slice against the grain. Pepper at the end, never before the sear.

name: Lamb Shoulder, Six Hours
why: Shoulder is the cheap cut with all the connective tissue in it. Time turns that into gelatin, which is exactly what you want and what a lean cut cannot give you.
steps: Salt the shoulder the night before and leave it uncovered in the fridge.
Sit it on halved onions and the head of garlic in a deep tray. Broth poured around, not over.
Cover tightly with a lid or two layers of foil. Oven at 140°C for five hours.
Uncover, turn the oven to 200°C, and give it 30 to 40 minutes to brown.
Rest 20 minutes. It should pull apart with a spoon. Spoon the fat from the tray back over it.

name: Charred Cabbage Wedge
why: Cabbage treated like a steak rather than a side. Hard char on the cut face, soft through the middle, and it stands up as the center of a plate.
steps: Cut two thick wedges through the core so the leaves stay attached.
Dry heavy pan, no oil, as hot as you dare. Cut face down, 5 minutes, until genuinely black.
Turn onto the other cut face, 4 minutes.
Add butter, mashed anchovy and garlic to the pan, cover, and cook 10 minutes on low, spooning the butter over.
Lemon, salt, pepper. The blackened part is the best part, do not trim it off.

name: Whole Cauliflower, Nothing Wasted
why: Leaves, core and florets all cook, all taste different, and all end up on the same plate. The leaves crisp like chips.
steps: Pull the outer leaves off and keep them. Trim the base flat so it sits.
Rub the whole head with melted ghee, salt and turmeric, getting it into the gaps.
Oven at 200°C for 35 minutes on its own.
Toss the leaves in ghee and salt and add them to the tray for the last 12 minutes, until they blacken at the tips.
Carve it in wedges. Olive oil and lemon at the table, crisped leaves on top.

name: Short Rib in Its Own Broth
why: The liquid it cooks in becomes the stock for two more meals. Nothing is thrown away and the second night is easier than the first.
steps: Salt the ribs hard, then brown them in tallow on every face. Take your time, this is where the color comes from.
Take them out. Brown the onions and carrots in the same fat.
Ribs back in, broth poured to two-thirds up, not covering them. Bay and garlic in.
Lid on, oven at 150°C, three hours. Turn them once at the halfway point.
Lift the meat out, skim the fat off the liquid and keep it. Keep the liquid too, it is stock now.

name: Confit Chicken Thigh
why: Submerged in fat and held low, the thigh goes soft all the way through and then crisps in seconds under heat. The fat is reusable for months.
ing: Enough tallow or ghee to cover
steps: Salt the thighs heavily and leave them in the fridge for 12 hours. Rinse and dry them completely.
Sit them in a deep oven dish with the garlic and thyme. Pour over melted fat until they are covered.
Oven at 130°C for two hours. It should never bubble hard, only the occasional lazy blip.
Lift them out and drain. They will be falling apart.
Skin-side down in a screaming hot dry pan for 90 seconds to crisp. Salt, pepper. Strain and keep the fat.

name: Liver, Onions, Vinegar
why: Vinegar hit into the hot pan cuts the iron edge that puts people off liver. It is the difference between eating it and enduring it.
steps: Slice the liver 1cm thick, salt it, and leave it out for 15 minutes.
Cook the onions in butter, low, for 15 minutes. Properly brown, not just softened.
Onions out. Pan up high. Liver in for 90 seconds a side and no more.
Liver out. A good splash of vinegar into the empty pan, let it hiss, scrape the base.
Onions back in to warm, pour it all over the liver, parsley and pepper. Rest two minutes.

name: Bison Burger, No Bun
why: The more you handle ground meat the tighter it gets. Shape it once, salt only the outside, and leave it alone in the pan.
steps: Divide the meat and shape it into two thick patties with as few movements as possible. Do not mix salt into it.
Salt the outside faces only, just before they hit the pan.
Tallow in a heavy pan, very hot. Patties in, and do not touch them for 3 minutes.
Turn once. Three minutes more. Press nothing, ever.
Rest 4 minutes. Wrap in lettuce leaves with mustard and raw onion.

name: Oysters and Cucumber
why: A light last meal that still carries dense minerals. Useful on a day you trained hard and do not want a heavy plate before sleep.
steps: Dice the cucumber very small and toss it with vinegar, minced shallot and pepper. Leave 10 minutes.
Shuck the oysters, keeping the liquor in the shell.
A small spoon of the cucumber on each.
Olive oil and lemon.
Eat them over ice if you have it, on a cold plate if you do not.

name: Mushrooms Confit in Butter
why: Mushrooms give up water first and take on fat second. Held low in butter for long enough they go dense and meaty instead of rubbery.
steps: Leave the mushrooms whole or halved. Do not slice them thin.
Butter, garlic and thyme in a wide pan on the lowest heat. Mushrooms in, one layer.
Thirty to forty minutes, turning occasionally. They will release water, then reabsorb the butter. Wait for the second part.
Salt only at the end. Salting early draws the water out too fast.
Lemon and pepper. Serve them as the whole plate, with an egg if you want more.

name: The Whole Leek
why: One vegetable, three techniques, nothing discarded. This is the restaurant method at its clearest and it costs about a pound.
ing: 4 leeks, whole, with roots and tops
steps: Separate each leek into three: the dark tops, the white middle, and the hairy root end. Wash all three carefully.
Char the tops black in a dry hot pan, then drop them into the olive oil and leave them to steep, overnight if possible, two hours at minimum.
Strain the oil. It is now dark green and smoky. Confit the white parts in it at 130°C for two and a half hours until completely soft.
Deep color the roots in a little of the same oil until crisp, then drain them on paper.
Plate the soft whites, spoon the smoky oil over, and scatter the crisped roots on top. Salt, lemon, pepper.

name: Beef and Bone Marrow
why: Marrow is the most fat-dense thing on the approved list and it turns a plain piece of beef into something you would pay for.
steps: Soak the marrow bones in salted cold water for an hour if you have time. It draws the blood out and keeps them pale.
Roast them cut-side up at 220°C for 15 to 20 minutes, until the marrow is loose and bubbling but has not run out.
Cook the beef as you like it while they roast, and rest it.
Chop parsley, shallot and lemon zest together into a rough, sharp salad.
Spoon marrow onto the beef, parsley over the top, watercress on the side. Salt heavily.

name: Brined Zucchini, Griddled
why: The same salting trick as the breakfast version, taken further with char and herbs. A vegetable plate that does not feel like a side.
steps: Slice thick, salt both sides, and leave in a colander for two hours. Do this in the morning.
Squeeze and dry them properly. They should feel firm, not wet.
Dry griddle, very hot, no oil. Three to four minutes a side without moving them, until barred black.
Straight into a bowl with sliced raw garlic, torn herbs, vinegar and a lot of olive oil while still hot.
Leave 10 minutes for it to soak in. Lemon and pepper at the table. Better cold the next day.

name: Dry-Brined Lamb Chops
why: Salt applied a day ahead goes all the way through and dries the surface, which is the only way to get a real crust on a small cut.
steps: Salt the chops on all faces and sit them uncovered on a rack in the fridge for 24 hours. Uncovered is the important word.
Take them out an hour before cooking. Do not rinse.
Render the fat edge first: stand the chops on their fat side in a hot dry pan, held together, for 3 minutes until it runs and browns.
Lay them flat, 2 minutes a side, with ghee, garlic and rosemary spooned over.
Rest for as long as they cooked. Lemon and pepper.

name: Asparagus, Brown Butter, Egg
why: Barely a recipe and still one of the better plates in the book. Proof that technique, not ingredients, is what most meals are missing.
steps: Snap the ends off and char the spears in a dry pan, rolling them, 5 minutes until blistered and still firm.
Brown the butter in a separate pan: past the foam, until the milk solids turn hazelnut and it smells nutty. Off the heat immediately, it goes from brown to burnt in seconds.
Soft-boil the eggs for 6 minutes and peel them under cold water.
Asparagus down, eggs broken over, brown butter poured across both.
Lemon, salt, pepper, crushed walnuts if you want the crunch.

name: Broth with Beef and Greens
why: When the stock is already made this is twenty minutes from nothing to a full meal, which is what makes it the one you actually cook on a bad night.
steps: Bring the broth up with sliced ginger and smashed garlic. Keep it just below a simmer for 10 minutes, then fish them out.
Slice the beef as thin as you can manage. Half-frozen meat slices thinner.
Greens into the broth for a minute.
Heat off. Beef into the hot liquid raw, and leave it for 60 seconds. It cooks in the residual heat and stays tender.
Coconut aminos, salt, spring onion. Eat it straight away.

name: Salmon and Rice Bowl
why: For the tiers still eating starch. The rice is a fist, not a plate, and it sits under the fish rather than being the point of the meal.
steps: Salt the salmon skin and dry it completely. Wet skin steams, dry skin crisps.
Ghee in a hot pan. Fish skin-side down, pressed flat for 10 seconds, then left alone for 4 minutes.
Turn it, 90 seconds, out of the pan. It carries on cooking while it rests.
Rice in the bowl first, then cucumber, avocado and a forkful of sauerkraut around the edge.
Salmon on top, skin up so it stays crisp. Coconut aminos and lemon.

name: Slow Beef with Squash
why: The squash goes in late so it holds its shape rather than dissolving, and it soaks up the fat from the beef instead of needing its own.
steps: Cut the beef into large chunks, salt them, and brown them hard in tallow in batches. Crowding the pan is why beef goes gray.
Onions in the same fat until dark. Beef back, broth to two-thirds up, bay and garlic.
Lid on, oven at 150°C, two hours.
Peel and chunk the squash and add it for the last 40 minutes only.
Skim the fat, keep it for cooking, and check the salt at the end rather than the start.

name: Sardines Grilled Over Bitter Greens
lineage: Francis Mallmann, parrilla. Fire and salt, nothing else.
why: Whole small fish over live fire, skin blistered, eaten with the greens underneath catching the fat.
steps: Get the grill hot enough that you cannot hold a hand over it for two seconds. Hot iron is what stops the skin sticking.
Salt the sardines on both sides and leave them 10 minutes. The salt pulls moisture to the surface so the skin dries and crisps.
Lay them on the grill. Leave them 4 minutes without touching them, then turn once and give them 3 more.
Pile the greens on the plate, put the fish on top while it is still hot, and pour the oil over both. The hot fish wilts the greens.
Lemon and salt at the table. To feed two, double the fish and the greens.

name: Mackerel Grilled Skin Side Down
lineage: Francis Mallmann, chapa. Skin against hot iron until it crisps.
why: Mackerel is oily enough to cook almost entirely on its skin side, which is where all the texture is.
steps: Pat the skin completely dry with a towel. Wet skin steams instead of crisping.
Salt the skin and rub the oil over it. Heat a heavy pan or flat grill to 220C, 425F.
Lay it skin down and press it flat for the first 10 seconds so the whole skin touches the metal.
Cook 5 to 6 minutes skin down without moving it. The flesh turns from clear to pale as it cooks up from the bottom.
Turn it for 30 seconds only, then plate skin up. Lemon and the sauerkraut cold on the side.

name: Salmon Collar in the Coals
lineage: Rasmus Munk, Plastic Fantastic. The collar is the best part and gets thrown away.
why: The collar is the piece behind the head, and it is the fattest part of the fish. Ask the counter for them and they are usually free.
steps: Let a fire burn down until the coals glow and no flame is left. Flame burns the fat before the collar cooks.
Salt the collars well and oil them lightly so they do not stick.
Lay them straight on the coals, skin side down, for 6 minutes.
Turn and give them 5 minutes more. The fat renders out and the skin blackens in places, which is what you want.
Eat them with your hands over the greens, with lemon. There is more meat in there than it looks.

name: Whole Mackerel in a Salt Crust
lineage: Francis Mallmann, salt-crusted fish. A salt shell steams the fish in its own juice.
why: The salt sets into a hard shell, so the fish cooks in its own moisture and comes out seasoned all through but not salty.
ing: 2 lb coarse unrefined mineral sea salt
steps: Heat the oven to 200C, 400F. Mix the salt with the egg white and a splash of water until it holds together like wet sand.
Put the thyme and lemon slices inside the fish.
Spread a finger-thick bed of salt on a tray, lay the fish on it, then pack the rest of the salt over the top so no fish shows.
Bake 22 minutes. Let it sit 5 minutes before you crack it, because it keeps cooking inside the shell.
Crack the crust with the back of a spoon and lift it off in pieces. Brush the loose salt away, peel the skin back, and lift the fillets off. Oil over the top.
One fish feeds one as a full plate, or two alongside vegetables.

name: Salmon Dry-Aged Three Days, Brown Butter
lineage: Ana Ros, Trout The Queen. Dry-age a fish, then finish it in browned butter.
why: Three days uncovered in the cold dries the surface and concentrates the flavor. Browned butter is the only sauce it needs.
ing: 5 oz wild salmon fillet, skin on
steps: Salt the fillet all over and set it on a rack over a plate, uncovered, in the coldest part of the fridge.
Leave it 3 days. The surface goes matte and slightly tacky. That dry surface is what browns properly.
Heat a dry pan to medium. Lay the fish skin down for 4 minutes, then turn it for 1 minute.

Lift the fish out. Put the butter in the same pan and swirl it until it smells like nuts and turns light brown, about 90 seconds. Take it off the heat the moment it colors, because it goes from brown to burnt fast.
Pour the butter over the fish and the greens. Lemon at the table.

name: Anchovies Cured in Salt and Vinegar
lineage: Jiro Ono, kohada. The same cure that made a cheap fish famous.
why: Salt firms the flesh and vinegar sets it. This is how a small oily fish becomes something you serve on purpose.
steps: Lay the fillets flat in one layer and cover them with the salt. Leave 45 minutes. The salt draws water out and firms them.
Rinse the salt off under cold water and pat dry.
Put them in a shallow dish and pour the vinegar over so they are just covered. Refrigerate 12 to 24 hours. They turn from pink to white, which is the sign they are done.
Lift them out, drain, and cover with the oil, garlic and parsley.
They keep 4 days in the oil in the fridge, so make a double batch and eat them across the week.

name: Sardine Rillettes in Butter
lineage: Joan Roca, Pig Trotter Carpaccio. Rich fish set in fat, sliced cold.
why: Mashed sardines set firm in butter, so you can cut them. Rich enough that a small piece is a meal with greens.
steps: Drain the sardines but keep the oil. Mash them with a fork, bones and all, because the bones soften to nothing and are the best part of the tin.
Work the soft butter into the fish until it is one paste. The butter is what sets it firm later.
Add the vinegar, zest, chives, a little pepper and salt. Taste it now, because cold food needs more salt than warm food.
Press it into a small dish, smooth the top, and pour a thin layer of the kept oil over to seal it.
Refrigerate 2 hours until firm. Cut in slices. Keeps 5 days sealed, and this quantity feeds two or three.

name: Mackerel Cured in Cider Vinegar
lineage: Jiro Ono, kohada. Vinegar firms the flesh and keeps it.
why: A cure instead of a cooking method. The fish comes out firm, sharp and ready to eat cold for days.
steps: Bury the fillets in the salt, skin up, for 30 minutes. This is the step that firms them.
Rinse well and dry. Any salt left behind makes the finished fish too strong.
Lay them in a dish and pour the vinegar over to cover. Refrigerate 4 hours.
Lift out, pat dry, and slice across the fillet at an angle into thin pieces.
Oil, pepper and dill over the top. Keeps 3 days. Half a fish is one lunch.

name: Oysters Warmed in Their Own Liquor
lineage: Joan Roca, Amontillado-steamed oyster. Gentle heat over their own liquid, no alcohol.
why: Barely warmed rather than cooked, in the seawater they came in. No wine, and none needed.
steps: Open the oysters over a bowl so you catch every drop of the liquor. That liquid is the whole sauce.
Loosen each oyster from its shell but leave it sitting in the shell.
Put the liquor, butter, shallot and vinegar in a small pan and warm it to just below a simmer, about 80C, 175F. Do not boil it, because boiling makes an oyster rubbery.
Spoon the warm liquid over the oysters in their shells and let them sit 60 seconds. They firm at the edges and stay soft in the middle.
Pepper and chives. Six is one lunch with greens beside it.

name: Beef Tongue, Pressed and Sliced Thin
lineage: Joan Roca, Pig Trotter Carpaccio. A collagen cut cooked, pressed, chilled, shaved.
why: A cut most people never buy, cooked until soft, pressed flat and sliced cold. It eats like something expensive.
steps: Cover the tongue with cold water in a pot with the onion, bay and salt. Bring it to a bare simmer.
Cook 3 hours at a bare simmer. A hard boil makes it tough. It is ready when a knife goes into the thick end with no resistance.
Lift it out and peel the skin off while it is still hot. It comes away in sheets now and will not come off at all once cold.
Wrap it tight in parchment, put it on a plate with something heavy on top, and refrigerate overnight. Pressing is what lets you slice it thin.
Slice as thin as you can. Oil, vinegar and parsley over the top. One tongue is six or seven lunches, so this is a cook-once cut.

name: Oxtail Cooked Long in Broth
lineage: Dabiz Munoz, Spanish Bull. An offcut as the centerpiece, not the filler.
why: Oxtail is mostly bone and connective tissue, and four hours turns all of that into something rich enough to coat a spoon.
steps: Salt the oxtail and brown it hard in the tallow on every side, about 10 minutes. The brown crust is where most of the flavor comes from.
Take the meat out. Cook the onion and carrot in the same fat for 5 minutes, scraping the bottom.
Put the meat back, pour the broth over, add the bay. The liquid should come halfway up, not cover it.
Lid on, oven at 150C, 300F, for 3.5 hours. It is done when the meat pulls off the bone with no effort.
Lift the meat out and boil the liquid down by half to thicken it. There is no flour in this, so reduction is the only thickener.
This makes two or three lunches and is better on the second day.

name: Beef Cheek in Its Own Juice
lineage: Joan Roca, low-temperature cooking. Long low heat turns collagen to silk.
why: Cheek is pure working muscle and full of collagen. Held low and long, the collagen melts and the meat goes silky.
steps: Salt the cheek and brown it in the tallow, 4 minutes a side.
Add the onion, garlic, broth and thyme. The liquid should come a third of the way up the meat.
Lid on, oven at 140C, 285F, for 3.5 hours. Low is the point. Above about 160C, 320F, the muscle tightens before the collagen has time to melt.
Check it with a spoon, not a knife. It is ready when a spoon breaks it apart.
Serve it in its own liquid with greens. One cheek is two lunches.

name: Marrow Roasted and Scooped Over Greens
lineage: Dabiz Munoz, Spanish Bull with marrow. Marrow is a fat and a sauce at once.
why: Marrow bones are cheap and mostly fat, and roasted marrow spread over bitter greens is a full plate.
steps: Heat the oven to 220C, 425F. Ask the counter to split the bones lengthwise, because you cannot do it at home.
Salt the cut face and roast them 15 to 18 minutes. They are ready when the marrow is soft and bubbling at the edges but has not run out of the bone.
Dress the greens with the vinegar and a little salt while the bones roast. The sharpness is there to cut the fat.
Scoop the marrow out with a small spoon and spread it over the greens. It melts into them.
Parsley and pepper over the top. Two bones is one lunch.

name: Lamb Neck, Four Hours
lineage: Joan Roca, low-temperature cooking. The cheapest cut wants the longest time.
why: Neck is the cut nobody asks for and it makes the best braise on the animal, because it is all collagen and bone.
steps: Salt the neck slices an hour ahead if you can. Salt needs time to reach the middle of a thick cut.
Brown them hard in the tallow, 5 minutes a side.
Add the onion, garlic, broth and rosemary. Lid on, oven at 150C, 300F.
Give it 3.5 hours. The meat should fall off the bone when you lift a piece.
Take the lid off for the last 20 minutes so the liquid thickens and the top colors.
Two slices is two lunches. The liquid sets to jelly in the fridge, which is the collagen, and it melts again when warmed.

name: Liver Grilled Fast Over Fire
lineage: Dabiz Munoz, bold spice on great protein. High heat and seconds, not minutes.
why: Liver turns dry and grainy the moment it is overdone. Very hot and very fast is the whole technique.
ing: 5 oz beef liver, sliced 1/2 inch thick
steps: Pat the liver completely dry and salt it. Dry surface, hot fire.
Get the grill or pan as hot as it goes, about 250C, 480F.
Rub the tallow on the liver, not the pan, so it does not smoke before the liver lands.
90 seconds a side and no more. The middle should still be pink. Cut into it to check, because liver goes from right to wrong in about 30 seconds.
Rest it 2 minutes, then slice it against the grain. Vinegar and greens on the side.

name: Chicken Thigh Dry-Brined and Air-Dried
lineage: Thomas Keller, roast chicken. Salt early, dry the skin, then high heat.
why: The salt goes in a day early and the skin dries uncovered overnight. That is the whole difference between crisp skin and soft skin.
ing: 2 pastured chicken thighs, bone in, skin on
steps: Salt the thighs all over, including under the skin, and set them on a rack in the fridge uncovered.
Leave them 12 to 24 hours. The salt seasons the meat all the way through and the air dries the skin out. Covered skin stays wet and will not crisp.
Heat the oven to 220C, 425F. Do not rinse or pat the thighs, because that puts the moisture back.
Oil them lightly, put the thyme underneath, and roast skin up 22 to 25 minutes until the skin is dark and tight.
Rest 5 minutes. Two thighs is one lunch, and the technique scales to a whole tray.

name: Chicken Thigh Poached in Butter
lineage: Thomas Keller, butter-poached lobster. Poaching in fat keeps lean meat soft.
why: Held in warm butter instead of water, the meat cannot dry out, because fat carries heat more gently than water does.
steps: Salt the thighs and leave them 15 minutes.
Melt the butter in a small pan with the garlic and thyme. Bring it to 75C, 165F, and hold it there. A thermometer matters here, because above 85C, 185F, the butter separates and the point is lost.
Slide the thighs in so the butter covers them. Add more butter or use a smaller pan if it does not.
Hold at that temperature 25 minutes. The meat goes opaque and stays soft.
Lift them out, salt again, and pepper. Keep the butter in the fridge and use it again for the same job.

name: Butter-Poached Salmon
lineage: Thomas Keller, butter-poached lobster. Fat as the poaching liquid, held low.
why: Salmon held in warm butter never gets the chalky white line that a hot pan gives it.
steps: Salt the salmon and leave it 10 minutes.
Melt the butter with the lemon peel and dill in a small pan and bring it to 60C, 140F.
Slide the fish in. It should be covered. Hold the temperature for 12 minutes.
It is done when it flakes under light pressure but is still deep pink in the middle. There is no browning and there is not meant to be.
Lift it out and spoon a little of the butter over. One fillet is one lunch.

name: Bone Broth Reduced to a Sauce
lineage: Yannick Alleno, extraction sauces. A sauce from bones, never from flour.
why: Four cups of broth boiled down to half a cup coats a spoon on its own. The thickener is the collagen already in it.
steps: Put the broth, shallot and thyme in a wide pan. Wide matters, because a wide pan reduces faster than a tall one.
Boil hard until it is down to about half a cup, 35 to 40 minutes. Skim any foam off the top as it rises.
Strain it and put it back on low heat.
Add the vinegar, then whisk the cold butter in off the heat. Off the heat is the point, because boiling now would split it.
Salt to taste. This is enough sauce for two plates of meat or vegetables, and it sets to jelly in the fridge.

name: Cold-Drawn Herb Sauce Over Beef
lineage: Yannick Alleno, cold extraction. Draw flavor cold so nothing is cooked away.
why: Herbs lose their top notes the moment they are heated. Drawn cold in oil and vinegar they keep all of it.
steps: Chop the herbs and garlic fine, put them in a jar with the oil, vinegar and salt, and leave it 20 minutes at room temperature. No heat at any point.
Salt the steak and cook it how you like it in a hot dry pan.
Rest the steak 5 minutes on the board. Resting lets the juices settle back instead of running out.
Slice it against the grain and spoon the cold sauce over the warm meat. The heat of the meat releases the herb smell at the table.
The sauce keeps 3 days and this makes enough for three plates.

name: Vegetable Broth Drawn Cold, Then Warmed
lineage: Yannick Alleno, La Balade Vegetale. Many vegetables, one clear liquid.
why: Vegetables steeped cold overnight give a clear, bright broth. Boiled, they give a dull one.
steps: Put all the vegetables and the water in a jar and refrigerate 8 hours or overnight. Nothing is cooked at this stage.
Strain it and throw the vegetables away. They have given up what they had.
Warm the liquid to 70C, 160F. Do not boil it, because boiling is what turns it dull and flat.
Salt it and pour the oil over the top of the bowl.
This makes four cups. Drink it as it is, or use it as the liquid in another dish.

name: Beef Carpaccio, Shaved Cold
lineage: Andoni Luis Aduriz, Veg Carpaccio. Thin and cold changes how a thing tastes.
why: The same beef eaten raw and paper thin tastes nothing like it does cooked. Freezing it briefly is what lets you cut it that thin.
ing: 5 oz grass-fed beef fillet, one piece
steps: Wrap the beef tight and freeze it 45 to 60 minutes. You want it firm to the squeeze, not frozen through.
Unwrap it and slice it as thin as you can with your sharpest knife. Firm meat is the only way to get slices this thin.
Lay the slices flat on a cold plate in one layer, barely touching.
Oil, lemon, salt and pepper over the top, then leave it 5 minutes. The lemon firms the surface slightly and the salt draws the flavor out.
Greens and parsley on top. Use beef you trust and eat it the day you buy it.

name: Warm Beef, Cold Kraut, One Plate
lineage: Andoni Luis Aduriz, Edible Stones. Temperature contrast as the whole idea.
why: Hot meat and cold ferment in the same mouthful. The contrast is the dish, not a garnish.
ing: 4 tbsp sauerkraut, cold from the jar
steps: Take the kraut out of the fridge only when you plate, so it stays properly cold.
Salt the steak and cook it in the tallow in a hot pan, 3 minutes a side for medium rare.
Rest it 5 minutes, then add the butter to the resting juices and spoon them back over.
Slice the steak and put it on the plate still hot. Put the cold kraut straight beside it, not on it, so the two do not meet until you eat them.
Pepper over the meat only. One steak is one lunch.

name: Cauliflower Carved Like a Roast
lineage: Rene Redzepi, Celeriac Shawarma. Roast a vegetable for hours and carve it.
why: A whole head roasted long enough goes sweet and dense all through, and you carve it in slices like meat.
ing: 1 small cauliflower, whole, leaves left on
steps: Heat the oven to 200C, 400F. Leave the leaves on, because they char and become the best part.
Cut the stem flat so it sits upright. Do not cut the head into florets. Whole is what makes the inside steam while the outside roasts.
Brush the butter all over, then the salt, turmeric and pepper.
Roast 50 minutes. Test it with a knife into the middle of the stem, which should go in with no resistance.
Let it sit 5 minutes, then carve it down through the head in thick slices. Oil over the cut faces. One small head is two lunches.

name: Cabbage in Layers, Roasted Long
lineage: Rene Redzepi, Celeriac Shawarma. Layers hold moisture, so they take long heat.
why: Cut in thick wedges and roasted slowly, cabbage goes sweet in the middle and black at the edges.
ing: Half a green cabbage, in 2 thick wedges
steps: Heat the oven to 190C, 375F. Cut through the core so each wedge holds together.
Brush the tallow into the cut faces and between the outer layers, and salt heavily.
Roast cut side down 40 minutes, then turn and give it 25 more. The layers steam inside while the faces color.
Vinegar over it in the last 5 minutes, which lifts the sweetness.
Butter and pepper at the table. Two wedges is one lunch, or a side for two.

name: Beets Salt-Baked with Anchovy
lineage: Mauro Colagreco, salt-crusted beetroot with caviar. A plain root plus one intense topping.
why: A salt crust cooks a beet in its own moisture so it tastes more like itself. One salty fish on top is all it needs.
ing: 2 lb coarse unrefined mineral sea salt
steps: Heat the oven to 200C, 400F. Mix the salt with the egg white and a little water until it holds shape.
Bury the beets completely in the salt on a tray. No beet should show, or that part dries out instead of steaming.
Bake 1 hour 15 minutes. Crack the crust and test with a skewer, which should slide in easily.
Break the crust off and rub the skins away with a towel while warm. They come off easily now.
Slice thick, lay the anchovies over, then the oil, vinegar and dill. Two beets is one lunch.

name: Radish and Beet, Raw and Salted
lineage: Mauro Colagreco, garden-first cooking. Vegetables treated like the main event.
why: Raw roots sliced thin and salted for ten minutes go from hard to crisp and sweet, with nothing cooked at all.
steps: Slice the radishes and beet as thin as you can. Thin is what makes raw root pleasant to eat.
Toss them with the salt and leave 10 minutes. The salt pulls water out and the slices firm up and lose their raw edge.
Pour off the water that has collected, which would otherwise dilute the dressing.
Dress with the oil and vinegar and toss again.
Pepper and torn mint over the top. Serve cold. This is one plate, and it does not keep.

name: Artichoke Braised in Olive Oil
lineage: Alain Ducasse, seasonal vegetable cookpot. Produce at the center, cooked slowly in fat.
why: Artichokes cooked slowly in oil rather than water keep everything they have, and the oil afterward is worth as much as the vegetable.
steps: Trim the tough outer leaves and the tips off the artichokes and halve them. Rub the cut faces with the lemon so they do not brown.
Put them in a small pan with the oil, garlic and bay. The oil should nearly cover them, so use a pan just big enough.
Cook on the lowest heat 35 to 40 minutes. It should never bubble hard. A bare shimmer is right, because hard bubbling fries them instead of braising them.
Test the base with a knife. It should be soft all the way through.
Salt and parsley. Keep the cooking oil in a jar and use it on everything for the next week.

name: Green Beans and Zucchini in Butter
lineage: Alain Ducasse, petits pois a la francaise. Braise the vegetables in fat, not water.
why: Cooked down slowly in butter with a little broth, summer vegetables go soft and sweet instead of squeaky.
steps: Melt the butter in a pan on medium low and add the beans and zucchini with a good pinch of salt.
Turn them in the butter 5 minutes without letting them brown. You are softening them, not searing them.
Add the broth and the shredded greens, put a lid on, and leave it 12 minutes on low. The greens collapse and thicken what is in the pan.
Take the lid off and cook 2 minutes more so what is left is buttery and not watery.
Pepper at the table. This is one lunch on its own or a side for two.

name: Brussels Sprouts Crisped in Tallow
lineage: Massimo Bottura, The Crunchy Part of the Lasagna. Cook for the crisp edge and nothing else.
why: The loose outer leaves burn crisp and the halves go soft. The whole point is to get as many crisp edges as possible.
steps: Heat the oven to 220C, 425F and put the tallow in a metal tray to melt in the oven.
Halve the sprouts and keep every loose leaf that falls off. Those leaves are the crisp part.
Toss everything in the hot fat and lay the halves cut side down in one layer. Crowding steams them instead of crisping them.
Roast 20 minutes without stirring. The cut faces go dark brown and the loose leaves go almost black.
Vinegar over them straight out of the oven, then salt and pepper. Two cups is one lunch or a side for two.

name: Liver, Butter, Thyme, Fast
lineage: Dan Barber, Everything from the Pig. Use the whole animal, including the organs.
why: Sliced thin and cooked in foaming butter for two minutes a side, liver is a weekday breakfast rather than a project.
ing: 5 oz beef liver, sliced 1/4 inch thick
steps: Slice the liver thin and pat it completely dry. Wet liver steams and goes grey.
Salt it. Heat the butter in a pan until it foams and the foam starts to subside.
Lay the slices in one layer with the thyme. Do not crowd them, because crowded liver boils in its own liquid.
2 minutes a side. Cut one open. It should still be pink in the middle.
Vinegar into the hot pan, swirl it once, and pour the pan over the liver and the greens.

name: Eggs Scrambled Over Broth
lineage: Ferran Adria, deconstructed Spanish omelette. Take a familiar dish apart and rebuild it.
why: The eggs are cooked in a bowl set over hot broth instead of in a pan, so they stay loose and never go rubbery.
steps: Bring the broth to a bare simmer in a small pan.
Beat the eggs in a metal bowl with the salt and sit the bowl on top of the pan. The bowl must not touch the broth, because indirect heat is what keeps the eggs soft.
Stir slowly and constantly with a spatula. It takes 5 to 6 minutes, which is slower than a pan and that is the point.
When it thickens to loose curds, take the bowl off and stir the butter in. It stops the cooking and holds it creamy.
Pour a little of the hot broth into a cup and drink it beside the eggs. Chives and pepper on top.

name: The Morning Plate, Taken Apart
lineage: Ferran Adria, deconstructed Spanish omelette. Same parts, new form, nothing added.
why: Every part of the usual plate, kept separate and at its own temperature, so you taste each one instead of a mixture.
steps: Boil the eggs 6 minutes exactly for a set white and a soft yolk, then put them straight into cold water so they stop cooking.
Slice the avocado and lay it in a line on the plate. Salt it on its own.
Dress the greens with the oil and a little salt, and put them in their own line beside it.
Kraut in a third line, cold from the jar.
Peel and halve the eggs and lay them at the end. Do not mix anything. Take a bit of each in turn and notice they taste different apart than together.

name: Mushrooms Dry-Roasted, Cool Yolk Over
lineage: Andoni Luis Aduriz, Broken Egg, Cool Yolk. Hot and cold on one plate on purpose.
why: The mushrooms come out of the oven hot and dry, and a cold raw yolk broken over them becomes the sauce.
steps: Heat the oven to 220C, 425F. Tear the mushrooms rather than slicing them, because torn edges catch more heat.
Put them on a dry tray with no fat and no salt and roast 15 minutes. They give up a lot of water first, and salt now would keep it in.
When the tray is dry, add the tallow and salt and roast 8 minutes more until the edges are brown.
Keep the yolks in the fridge until the moment you plate, so they are properly cold.
Tip the hot mushrooms into a bowl, break the cold yolks over them, and stir once. Pepper and parsley.

name: Leeks in the Embers, Yolk Sauce
lineage: Grant Achatz, aroma as an ingredient. Ash and smoke as seasoning.
why: Whole leeks go straight into the coals until the outside is black. The inside steams sweet and tastes of smoke.
ing: 3 whole leeks, roots trimmed, tops left on
steps: Let a fire burn down to glowing coals. Put the leeks straight on them, unwrapped and unoiled.
Turn them every 5 minutes for about 25 minutes. The outside goes completely black, which is meant to happen and is not the part you eat.
While they cook, whisk the yolks with the vinegar and a pinch of salt, then add the oil a drop at a time, whisking, until it thickens. Adding oil slowly is what stops it splitting.
Take the leeks off and let them sit 5 minutes. Peel the burnt outer layers away and the soft pale inside slides out.
Salt the leeks, pepper them, and spoon the yolk sauce over. Three leeks is one breakfast.

name: Eggs Under Smoked Rosemary
lineage: Grant Achatz, tableside aroma. Aroma arrives before the food does.
why: A sprig of rosemary lit and put under a bowl fills the eggs with smoke without cooking them any further.
steps: Cook the eggs softly in the butter in a pan on low heat, taking them off while they still look slightly underdone. They keep cooking on the plate.
Put them on a plate and set a large bowl upside down nearby.
Light the end of one rosemary sprig at the stove, blow the flame out, and let it smoke. Put it on the plate beside the eggs.
Cover both with the bowl and leave it 2 minutes. The smoke has nowhere to go and settles into the eggs.
Lift the bowl at the table so the smoke comes out as you sit down. Take the rosemary off, then salt and pepper.

name: White Rice, Broth, Egg
lineage: Virgilio Martinez, Lofty Andes. Build the plate from one place and one season.
why: Rice cooked in bone broth instead of water takes all of it in. Intermediate and Beginner only, because this tier has starch.
steps: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear, which stops it going sticky.
Put it in a pan with the broth and a pinch of salt. Bring it to a boil, then turn it to the lowest heat and put the lid on.
15 minutes, lid on the whole time. Do not lift it, because the steam is doing the cooking.
Take it off the heat and leave it 5 minutes, still covered. Then stir the butter through.
Make a well in the middle, break the egg into it, and cover again for 3 minutes. The heat of the rice sets the white and leaves the yolk soft.
Chives on top. This is one breakfast and it doubles cleanly.

name: Cured Sardine, Egg Yolk, Chive
lineage: Jiro Ono, kohada cured in salt and vinegar. Salt and vinegar curing makes a small oily fish the center of the plate.
why: A two hour cure turns a tinned or fresh sardine firm and bright, and a raw yolk over it is the whole sauce.
steps: Lay the fillets flat, cover them with the salt, and leave 30 minutes. This firms them.
Rinse and dry, then cover with the vinegar and refrigerate 90 minutes. They turn from translucent to white.
Lift them out and pat dry. Lay them on a cold plate.
Break the yolk over the middle and add the oil. Break the yolk at the table, not before, so it is still whole when it arrives.
Chives and pepper. Four fillets is one breakfast.

name: Raw Salmon Pounded Thin
lineage: Eric Ripert, Thinly Pounded Yellowfin Tuna. Pound a raw fillet thin so it eats like a luxury.
why: Pounded between two sheets until it is almost transparent, raw salmon changes texture completely and needs only oil and salt.
steps: Slice the salmon into thin pieces and lay them between two sheets of parchment.
Pound them gently and evenly with the flat of a heavy pan until they are almost see through. Gently is the word, because hard pounding tears it.
Peel the top sheet off and turn the salmon straight onto a cold plate.
Oil over the whole surface, then salt, then a little lemon. Salt it just before eating, because salt on raw fish starts to cure it within minutes.
Pepper and chives. Use fish you trust and eat it the day you buy it.

name: Beets in a Salt Crust, Cold, with Egg
lineage: Mauro Colagreco, salt-crusted beetroot. A salt crust cooks a root in its own moisture.
why: Bake the beets the night before and this is a five minute breakfast in the morning.
ing: 2 lb coarse unrefined mineral sea salt
steps: Heat the oven to 200C, 400F. Mix the salt with the egg white and a little water until it holds shape.
Bury the beets completely and bake 1 hour 15 minutes, then cool them in the crust and refrigerate overnight.
In the morning, crack the crust, rub the skins off, and slice the beets thick.
Boil the eggs 7 minutes, then cool them in cold water and peel them.
Beets on the plate, eggs halved on top, oil and vinegar over, dill last. Everything cold except nothing, which is the point of doing it the night before.

name: Beef Wrapped in Duxelles, Seared
lineage: Gordon Ramsay, Beef Wellington. The dish works without the pastry.
why: Everything that makes a Wellington taste like a Wellington is the mushroom layer, not the pastry. So this is the mushroom layer and the beef.
ing: 6 oz grass-fed beef fillet, one piece
steps: Chop the mushrooms as fine as you can, almost to a paste. Cook them in the butter with the shallot, garlic and thyme on medium heat.
Keep cooking, 20 to 25 minutes, until all the water has gone and it is a dark thick paste. This is duxelles, and it is not ready until the pan is dry.
Salt the beef hard and sear it in a very hot dry pan, 1 minute on every side including the ends.
Take it off the heat and press the duxelles all over the outside in a thick even layer while the meat is still hot, so it sticks.
Oven at 200C, 400F, for 8 minutes for medium rare. Rest it 8 minutes before cutting, or the juices run out and take the coating with them.
Cut in thick slices. One piece is one dinner.

name: Lamb Wrapped in Mushroom and Herbs
lineage: Gordon Ramsay, Beef Wellington. A mushroom layer seasons and protects the meat.
why: The same idea on lamb, with rosemary in the coating, so the outside is dark and herbal and the inside stays pink.
steps: Cook the mushrooms, garlic and rosemary in the butter until the pan is completely dry, about 20 minutes.
Salt the lamb and sear it in the tallow, 90 seconds a side, until the outside is brown all over.
Press the mushroom mixture over the whole surface while the lamb is hot.
Oven at 200C, 400F, for 7 minutes. Lamb loin is lean, so a minute too long is the difference between pink and grey.
Rest 8 minutes, then slice thick. One piece feeds one, or two as part of a bigger plate.

name: Oysters Seared Hard in Butter
lineage: Gordon Ramsay, pan-seared scallops. A dry pan, high heat, one turn.
why: Oysters out of the shell and seared hard for forty seconds a side go firm and brown outside and stay soft inside.
steps: Drain the oysters well and pat them dry on a towel. Wet oysters will not brown, they will steam.
Get a heavy pan very hot, about 230C, 450F, then add the butter and wait for the foam to subside.
Lay the oysters in with space between them and do not move them for 40 seconds.
Turn each one once and give it 30 seconds more. They firm up and take a brown edge.
Off the heat, lemon into the pan, then pour the pan butter over. Salt, pepper and parsley. Eight is one dinner with greens.

name: Wild Game Roasted Rare
lineage: Dan Barber, whole farm cooking. Cook what the land near you actually gives.
why: Game is leaner than beef, so it wants a hot oven, a short time and a long rest. Whatever is local where you are is the right animal.
ing: 8 oz venison or other wild game loin
steps: Salt the loin and leave it out of the fridge 30 minutes. Cold meat into a hot oven cooks unevenly.
Sear it in the tallow in a hot pan, 90 seconds a side.
Add the thyme, garlic and butter to the pan and spoon the foaming butter over the meat for 30 seconds.
Oven at 220C, 425F, for 6 to 8 minutes. Game has almost no fat to protect it, so pull it at rare and let the rest finish it.
Rest 10 minutes, which is longer than the cooking. Slice thin against the grain.

name: Everything From the Animal, One Board
lineage: Dan Barber, Everything from the Pig. One animal, several cuts, one plate.
why: Liver, marrow and a piece of steak from the same animal on one board, so you see how different the same animal tastes.
steps: Oven to 220C, 425F. Roast the marrow bone 16 minutes, until soft and bubbling but not run out.
While it roasts, salt the steak and the liver and dry both well.
Cook the steak in the tallow, 3 minutes a side, and rest it.
Same pan, higher heat, liver in for 90 seconds a side only. Liver goes grainy in seconds, so it is always last and always fast.
Vinegar in the pan, swirl, and pour over the greens. Lay all three on a board with the marrow still in the bone and a spoon beside it.
Salt and parsley at the table. This board feeds two.

name: The Whole Farm Plate
lineage: Dan Barber, Vegetables on a Fence. Greens, an egg and broth from one place.
why: Whatever greens are good near you, a good egg and broth. The plate changes with the month and the method does not.
steps: Cook the leek and garlic in the butter on low 8 minutes until soft and not colored.
Add the broth and bring it to a bare simmer.
Add the greens a handful at a time, letting each one wilt before the next. All at once and they cool the pan and stew.
Make two wells and break the eggs in. Lid on, 4 minutes, until the whites are set and the yolks are not.
Salt and pepper. Eat it out of the bowl with the broth. This is one dinner, or two smaller ones.

name: Mackerel Roasted at an Exact Heat
lineage: Heston Blumenthal, precise temperatures. Write the temperature down and hold it.
why: Oily fish held at a low exact temperature stays translucent and silky instead of flaking apart. The number is the recipe.
steps: Salt the fillet and leave it 15 minutes, then pat the surface dry.
Heat the oven to 110C, 230F. This is much lower than fish is usually roasted and it is the whole method.
Put the fish in an oiled dish with the lemon peel and thyme, skin up.

Roast 14 to 16 minutes. Take it out when the thickest part reads 45C, 113F, on a thermometer. Without a thermometer, it is ready when the flesh has just turned from glassy to opaque and still resists a fork.
Oil and pepper over the top. It will look underdone next to fish you have roasted hot, and it is not.

name: Triple-Cooked Sweet Potato
lineage: Heston Blumenthal, Triple-Cooked Chips. Three stages build a texture one cannot.
why: Simmer, chill, roast, chill, roast again. Each stage does a different job and the result is crisp outside and fluffy in. Intermediate and Beginner only.
ing: 1 large sweet potato, in thick batons
steps: Simmer the batons in salted water 8 minutes, until the edges just start to break. This cooks the inside, which roasting alone cannot do without burning the outside.
Drain them and leave them on a rack 30 minutes to dry and cool. The surface must go completely dry, because steam is what stops a crust forming.
Roast in the tallow at 180C, 350F, for 15 minutes. Take them out and cool them again, 20 minutes.
Roast a second time at 220C, 425F, for 12 minutes with the rosemary. The second roast is the one that makes the shell.
Salt straight out of the oven. This serves two, and the first two stages can be done a day ahead.

name: Burnt Onion and Bone Broth
lineage: Ferran Adria, deconstruction. A familiar soup rebuilt from two things.
why: Onion soup without the bread, the cheese or the wine. Two ingredients, and the depth comes from taking the onions further than feels right.
steps: Cook the onions in the butter on medium low with a pinch of salt, stirring every few minutes.
Keep going 35 to 40 minutes. They go clear, then gold, then deep brown. Brown is where the flavor is, and most people stop ten minutes early.
Let a few catch and blacken on the bottom of the pan, then scrape them back in. That bitterness is what replaces the wine.
Add the broth, the thyme and the vinegar and simmer 15 minutes.
Salt and pepper. No bread and no cheese, and it does not need either. This makes two bowls.

name: Whole Fish Between Two Fires
lineage: Francis Mallmann, al infiernillo. Heat above and below cooks a whole fish evenly.
why: Fire underneath and fire above, so a whole fish cooks from both sides at once and never has to be turned.
ing: 1 whole mackerel, about 1.5 lb, gutted and scaled
steps: Build two fires and let both burn to coals. Set a grate over the first and put a metal tray of coals above it, or use a lidded grill with coals top and bottom.
Salt the mackerel inside and out and fill the cavity with the lemon and thyme.
Oil the fish and lay it on the grate. Close the heat above it.
22 to 25 minutes without turning it. Turning a whole fish is when it breaks, and heat from both sides means you never have to.
It is done when the flesh at the thickest part lifts cleanly off the bone. Oil and pepper over it, and serve it whole at the table. One fish feeds two.
